title: Physics-informed neural networks for PDE problems: a comprehensive review
authors_full: Kuang Luo, Jingshang Zhao, Ying-Ping Wang, Jiayao Li, Junjie Wen, Jiong Liang, Henry Soekmadji, Shaolin Liao
affiliations: School of Electronics and Information Technology, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, Guangdong, China (Luo, Zhao, Wang, Li, Wen, Liang, Liao); Collins Aerospace, Rockford, IL, USA (Soekmadji)
pdf_path: E:/University/11th_trimester/pinn-review/papers/pdf/PINN-A17.md (full text captured from the Springer online version, CC BY-NC-ND, via reader proxy; direct PDF download blocked by bot challenge, so no local PDF)
subdomain: PINN methodology for generic PDE problems: architectures (MLP/CNN/RNN/GAN/KAN/Transformer/NAS/domain decomposition), activation functions, adaptive data resampling, loss design and reweighting, feature embedding; brief application survey (fluids, solid mechanics, EM/optics) and software overview
industry_context: Cross-domain academic review; no company/lab is attached to any application discussed; motivating sectors named are aerospace engineering and meteorology (Sec. 1); one co-author is from Collins Aerospace (Rockford, IL, USA)
problem_class: survey (covers forward and inverse PDE problems, with operator learning as an outlook direction)
physics_enforced_exact: Canonical PINN formulation (Eq. 3): PDE residual f(x, t, du/dx, du/dt, lambda) = 0 for x in Omega, t in [0,T], with initial condition u(x,0) = h(x) on Omega and boundary condition u(x,t) = g(x,t) on dOmega. Concrete instances surveyed: Navier-Stokes for fluid motion (Sec. 3.1), 1D Poisson -Delta u = sum_{k=1}^{3} k sin(kx) + 7 sin(7x) + 8 sin(8x), x in [0,pi], with Dirichlet u(x=0)=0, u(x=pi)=pi (Eq. 32), plus heat, Burgers, Schroedinger, Allen-Cahn, KdV, damped wave, advection-diffusion, 3D Helmholtz, and solid-mechanics elasticity equations
pde_type: multiple (elliptic: Poisson, Helmholtz; parabolic: heat, diffusion, Burgers, Allen-Cahn; hyperbolic: wave, KdV; stochastic DEs in the GAN-based variants)
dimensionality: 1D to 3D examples (1D Poisson/Burgers; 2D heat; 3D wake flows, 3D Helmholtz); high-dimensional cited up to 50 dimensions (Zeng et al. 2022 adaptive DNNs)
nonlinearity: mixed (reviews linear Poisson/Helmholtz/wave cases through strongly nonlinear Navier-Stokes, Allen-Cahn cubic reaction, nonlinear hyperelasticity, and multi-scale problems)
bcs_ic_handled: In the reviewed baseline, IC and BC are soft L2 penalties: L_b matches u~(x_b,t) to g on dOmega and L_i matches u~(x_i,0) to h, each weighted by w_b and w_i (Eqs. 5-6). Reviewed variants include soft-and-hard boundary constraints using Fourier expansions (Li et al. 2024a), per-point trainable self-adaptive weights on IC/BC losses (SA-PINNs), and domain-decomposition interface continuity u_i = u_j on Gamma_ij (Eq. 19)
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty (the review's canonical scheme: automatic-differentiation PDE residual plus IC/BC penalty terms in a weighted sum); hard-constraint Fourier-based BC treatments and per-point adaptive weighting are surveyed, but weak/variational forms are not a treated category
enforcement_details: Physics enters by automatic differentiation of the network output u~(x,t;theta) inside the residual f evaluated at collocation points T_f; total loss L = L_physics + L_data (Eq. 4) with L_physics = w_f L_f + w_b L_b + w_i L_i (Eq. 5), each term an MSE over T_f/T_b/T_i samples (Eq. 6), plus data MSE over T_d (Eq. 7). Surveyed enrichments: residual-gradient loss terms |df/dx_i|^2 (gPINN, Eqs. 25-29), interface losses sum_{i!=j} L_interface^{ij} (Eq. 20), Gaussian-likelihood loss reweighting (lbPINN, Eqs. 21-24), input feature embeddings (Fourier feature mapping gamma(v), Eq. 31; sinusoidal mappings; prior dictionaries; DaPINN replica/power-series/Fourier-series input augmentation), L-infinity min-max loss for HJB equations, and adversarial discriminator losses in GAN-based UQ
network_architecture: Survey of: MLP/FNN - vanilla PINN used a 5-layer FNN with 100 neurons/layer for Schroedinger and 4-layer, 200-neuron FNN for Allen-Cahn (Sec. 2.1.1); CNN - PhyGeoNet, hybrid CNN-FVM, Spline-PINN, PICNN, f-PICNN; CNN-LSTM - PhyCRNet encoder-decoder ConvLSTM, peridynamic CNN-LSTM; GAN - PI-GANs, WGAN-UQ; KAN - KINN, Chebyshev KANs, PIKANs with adaptive grid training; Transformer - PIT, PINNsFormer, Transolver (PhysicsAttention); NAS - Auto-PINN, NAS-PINN (bi-level optimization); Separable PINN (forward-mode AD, axis-by-axis); PirateNets (residual adaptive networks); domain decomposition - XPINN, cPINN, improved DD-DNN
activation_function: tanh and sigmoid as common choices; sin (sinusoidal mappings, sf-PINN; Wavelet activation in PINNsFormer); adaptive activations with trainable scaling parameter (Jagtap et al. 2020b); physics-informed kernel functions as custom activations (PIKFNN); physical activation functions PAFs derived from the PDE's mathematical expressions (Abbasi & Andersen 2024)
input_representation: (x,t) spatio-temporal coordinates as the baseline input; surveyed augmentations: Fourier feature mappings (Eq. 31), multi-scale spatio-temporal Fourier features, sinusoidal input mappings (sf-PINN), task-dependent prior dictionaries (PD-PINN), dimension augmentation via replica/power-series/Fourier-series extensions (DaPINN), axis-by-axis inputs (Separable PINN)
output_representation: solution field(s) u(x,t) directly (velocity/pressure fields in fluid cases; full velocity and pressure reconstructed from sparse observations in hemodynamics/high-speed flows; constitutive parameters and geometric topology in inverse solid-mechanics cases); stochastic solution fields generated by GAN generators in PI-GAN/WGAN-UQ variants; no output-transform category is surveyed
loss_terms: L = L_physics + L_data (Eq. 4); L_physics = w_f L_f(theta;T_f) + w_b L_b(theta;T_b) + w_i L_i(theta;T_i) (Eq. 5) with the three MSE terms of Eq. 6; L_data = (1/|T_d|) sum |u~(x_d,t;theta) - u(x_d,t)|^2 (Eq. 7); gPINN: L = w_f L_f + w_b L_b + w_i L_i + sum_{i=1}^d w_{g_i} L_{g_i} (Eq. 25); lbPINN: L = (1/2e_f^2) L_PDE + (1/2e_b^2) L_BC + (1/2e_i^2) L_IC + (1/2e_d^2) L_data + log e_f e_b e_i e_d (Eq. 24); DD: L = sum_i L_physics^i + sum_{i!=j} L_interface^{ij} (Eq. 20)
loss_weighting: surveyed progression: fixed weights (baseline) -> learning-rate annealing using gradient statistics (Wang et al. 2021c) -> NTK-eigenvalue-based balancing (Wang et al. 2022a) -> self-adaptive loss balancing via maximum-likelihood uncertainty parameters (lbPINNs, Xiang et al. 2022) -> per-point fully trainable self-adaptive weights (SA-PINNs, McClenny & Braga-Neto 2023) -> loss-attentional networks with adversarial descent/ascent weighting (LA-PINN, Song et al. 2024) and self-paced SelectNet (Gu et al. 2021)
sampling_strategy: static: uniform, random, Latin hypercube, Halton, Hammersley and Sobol sequences; resampling every few iterations (DeepXDE); adaptive surveyed: RAR residual-based adaptive refinement (DeepXDE, first adaptive method), importance sampling proportional to the loss (Nabian et al. 2021), RAD and RAR-D (Wu et al. 2023), R3 retain-resample-release against propagation failures (Daw et al. 2023), DAS-PINNs with KRnet generative sampling of the residual PDF, DMIS dynamic mesh importance sampling, GAS Gaussian-mixture adaptive sampling, PINNACLE joint collocation+experimental point selection, AAS adversarial adaptive sampling unifying PINNs and optimal transport; authors' own hybrid adaptive (HA) sampling combining randomness with residual-based selection (Luo et al. 2025), demonstrated on 1D Poisson with N_r = 14/26 residual points at 20k/40k epochs, 10 repeats (Table 3, Fig. 10)
optimizer_schedule: review states Adam and L-BFGS are the traditional optimizers and that they 'may struggle to converge efficiently' for fast-varying/high-frequency solutions (Sec. 5.1); HA-sampling example trained for 20,000 and 40,000 epochs (Table 3); no global optimizer schedule is prescribed (review paper)
domain_decomposition: covered as an architecture class (Sec. 2.1.8): Omega = union of N subdomains Omega_i, physics F_i(u_i) = 0 solved per subdomain, interface condition u_i = u_j on Gamma_ij, composite loss sum of subdomain physics losses plus interface losses (Eqs. 17-20); XPINN: generalized space-time domain decomposition, arbitrary decomposition, separate network per subdomain with per-subdomain hyperparameters enabling parallel training; cPINN: flux continuity across interfaces for conservation laws with per-subdomain optimizer/activation/width choices; improved DD-DNN (Wu et al. 2022) targets single-network limitations and gradient pathology on large-scale problems
uq_method: Wasserstein GAN-based uncertainty quantification of PDE solutions with groupsort-activation discriminators (Gao & Ng 2022); physics-informed GANs encoding stochastic differential equations for forward/inverse/mixed stochastic problems (Yang et al. 2020) - the only UQ threads surveyed
data_regime: review spans physics-only training ('without requiring labeled data': PhyGeoNet, Spline-PINN, f-PICNN, PhyCRNet, Rao et al. elastodynamics), sparse experimental measurements (planar PIV, non-invasive 4D flow MRI in hemodynamics, density gradients and surface pressure in high-speed flows), and simulation-generated data; no unified data regime - it is a survey
datasets_used: Benchmark equations discussed: 1D Poisson (Table 3, Figs. 12), heat, Burgers (Figs. 7, 13), Schroedinger, Allen-Cahn, KdV, damped wave, Navier-Stokes, advection-diffusion, 3D Helmholtz, spatiotemporal PDEs (PhyCRNet); Transolver evaluated across six benchmarks plus large-scale industrial simulations; the review names no consolidated public benchmark suite
baselines_compared: classical solvers discussed as context: FEM, FVM, FDM, particle-based methods, Finite Cell Method (Sec. 1); PINN vs PINN-variant comparisons surveyed: vanilla PINN vs Random-R/RAD/HA resampling on 1D Poisson (Table 3); PIT vs DeepONet and Wang et al. 2021c on 1D Burgers and 2D heat; KAN vs MLP (Shukla et al. 2024 FAIR comparison); PhyCRNet vs existing PINNs; Guo et al. 2022 reports PINNs superior to FDM and FEM on highly non-uniform forward solid-mechanics problems
evaluation_metrics: L2 relative error (Eq. 8), RMSE (Eq. 9) and PDE residual (Eq. 10) formalized in Sec. 1.1.2 as the standard metrics; Table 3 reports L2 relative error mean +/- std over 10 repeats
key_quantitative_results: - The review's only original experiment (HA sampling, 1D Poisson Eq. 32, 10 repeats, L2 relative error): PINN HA (ours) 2.73% +/- 2.38% (N_r=14, 20k epochs), 0.24% +/- 0.21% (N_r=26, 20k), 1.28% +/- 0.76% (N_r=14, 40k), 0.11% +/- 0.08% (N_r=26, 40k) vs vanilla PINN 18.07% +/- 3.70%, 6.82% +/- 4.11%, 48.28% +/- 36.22%, 15.30% +/- 13.95% and Random-R 3.76% +/- 2.02%, 0.99%, 2.52% +/- 1.89%, 0.14% (Table 3). - Sec. 5.1 pegs current PINN convergence accuracy 'around 10^-3' and calls for rigorous analysis. - Cited claims: Wang et al. 2021c learning-rate annealing improves accuracy by factors of 50-100x across computational physics problems; Zeng et al. 2022 adaptive loss/activation/sampling reaches relative errors O(10^-4) on some 50-dimensional problems; PAFs reduce network size by up to 75% at maintained accuracy (Abbasi & Andersen 2024); Transolver achieves a 22% relative gain across six benchmarks (Wu et al. 2024); sf-PINN improves model accuracy by a few orders of magnitude (Wong et al. 2024).
speedup_claims: Cited, not measured: Separable PINNs 'substantially reduce training run-times' at comparable accuracy; PIT delivers significantly improved solving performance at computational cost similar to DeepONet; adaptive activation functions accelerate convergence, especially early in training; PAFs cut network size by up to 75%; HA sampling outperforms state-of-the-art resampling (Table 3). The review itself claims no wall-clock speedup vs FEM/FVM.
ablations: None by the review beyond its Table 3 sampling comparison (HA vs vanilla PINN vs Random-R vs RAD at two point counts x two epoch budgets, 10 repeats each). Surveyed component studies: network-size sensitivity - 'employing excessively small or large sizes for PINNs can lead to diminished performance' (He et al. 2020); MLP vs KAN FAIR comparison - original B-spline KANs struggle with accuracy/efficiency, Chebyshev KANs match MLPs but can diverge under certain conditions (Shukla et al. 2024).
stated_limitations: Sec. 5.1: slow convergence, sensitivity to hyperparameters, difficulty scaling to high-dimensional or multi-physics problems; current accuracy plateau 'around 10^-3'; 'gradient pathologies' from numerical stiffness causing imbalanced gradients (per Krishnapriyan et al. 2021); difficulty capturing fast-varying or high-frequency solutions where Adam/L-BFGS struggle; multi-physics interaction complexity beyond current optimization; inefficiency with noisy or incomplete data; lack of valuable experimental datasets with corresponding physical models and parameters. Sec. 5.2: reliance on manual formulation of physical constraints ('cumbersome and challenging for problems with complex or unknown physics'); high sensitivity to architecture, training strategies and BC handling requiring substantial tuning. Sec. 6: need for larger batch sizes, sophisticated training procedures, and handling of high-dimensional and non-linear problems.
failure_modes: Surveyed failure mechanisms: 'gradient pathologies' due to numerical stiffness producing imbalanced gradients that impede simultaneous satisfaction of PDE constraints and BCs, yielding suboptimal solutions (Krishnapriyan et al. 2021); imbalanced convergence rates across loss components revealed by NTK analysis (Wang et al. 2022a); 'propagation failures' with imbalanced PDE residual fields causing convergence to trivial solutions, mitigated by R3 sampling (Daw et al. 2023); spectral bias restricting learning of high-frequency functions (Rahaman et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2021a); the 'loss-jump' phenomenon - significant solution deviation when switching from data loss to model loss due to differing frequency preferences (Wang et al. 2024d); L2 loss instability for HJB equations, motivating L-infinity min-max training (Wang et al. 2022b); single-network gradient pathology on large-scale problems (Wu et al. 2022)
reproducibility: Sec. 4 (Table 4) surveys open-source frameworks with backends: DeepXDE (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX), IDRLnet (PyTorch), NeuroDiffEq (PyTorch), SciANN (TensorFlow), TensorDiffEq (TensorFlow; described as 'the only fully open-source multi-GPU PINN solution suite', with full self-adaptive solver support). The review itself releases no code, data, or configuration; HA-sampling example refers to Luo et al. 2025 (Appl Intell 55(4):255)
quotable_finding: However, the complexity of managing these components in practice often leads to issues such as slow convergence, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and difficulty in scaling to high-dimensional or multi-physics problems. (Sec. 5.1; online version has no page pagination)
relevance_rqs: RQ4 (reviews+reliability): the primary positioning target - the most-cited 2025 comprehensive PINN review (slices A+G); our survey must explicitly differentiate from its scope (method-centric, thin applications, no quantitative meta-analysis, no reliability evidence tables); RQ2 (components): Table 2 taxonomy of architectures/resampling/loss/embedding is the reference component classification to extend; RQ3 (physics+mechanism): codifies the canonical soft-penalty autodiff-residual mechanism (Eqs. 3-7) that our mechanism column must generalize; RQ1 (industries/problem classes): only three application domains sketched in one paragraph each (fluids, solid mechanics, EM/optics) - leaving the cross-industry mapping our survey provides
manuscript_section: Introduction/related-work paragraph differentiating our survey from existing reviews (S2); S4 methods taxonomy cross-check (architectures, sampling, loss weighting, embedding); T1/T2 component tables (taxonomy and training-method rows); tooling paragraph in S4 or S6 (Table 4 frameworks); reliability/challenges discussion (accuracy plateau, failure modes)
cross_paper_links: builds-on PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis 2019, cited CR99 throughout as the foundational PINN; vanilla-PINN architectures/benchmarks reused as reference); reviews PINN-B12 (DeepONet, Lu et al. 2021a CR73) in Sec. 2.1.6 (PIT comparison) and Sec. 5.2 operator-learning outlook, plus physics-informed DeepONet (Wang et al. 2021b); reviews PINN-B07 (XPINN, cited CR53 as the generalized space-time DD method; generalization analyzed via Hu et al. 2022) and cPINN (Jagtap et al. 2020a); reviews PINN-A07 (SA-PINNs, McClenny & Braga-Neto 2023 CR78) in the loss-reweighting section; reviews PINN-A06 (Wang, Yu & Perdikaris 2022a NTK perspective, CR127) for loss balancing and training failure; also cites Krishnapriyan et al. 2021 failure modes (cf. PINN-A03), Jacot et al. NTK, DeepXDE (Lu et al. 2021b), PirateNets, KAN/KINN, Transolver, PhyCRNet, PhyGeoNet. NOTABLE OMISSION: FNO (PINN-B13) is never cited - operator learning cites only DeepONet, physics-informed DeepONet, and Spherical FNO (Bonev et al. 2023). Self-citations: HA sampling (Luo et al. 2025) and DaPINN (Guan et al. 2023, shared author S.-L. Liao) are promoted as the review's own contributions.
notes_caveats: Analyzed from the Springer online full text (CC BY-NC-ND) captured via a reader proxy after both direct PDF download and landing-page fetch were blocked by a JavaScript bot challenge; the complete running text of all 6 sections plus the full contents of Tables 2-4 were read, but figures (image-based) were not inspected and the typeset PDF pagination is unavailable, so locators use section/equation numbers (article is Artif Intell Rev 58, article no. 323). Scope caveat for positioning: despite the title, 'comprehensive' is generous - Sec. 3 (Applications) is ~1 page covering only fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and electromagnetics/optics, with no thermal, energy, battery, nuclear, climate or geoscience coverage despite the introduction citing those fields; there is no quantitative meta-analysis, no accuracy-vs-method summary table, and the only original numbers are the authors' own HA-sampling Poisson demo. Self-promotion bias: HA sampling (Luo et al. 2025) and DaPINN (Guan et al. 2023) are highlighted as the recommended solutions in Secs. 2.2/2.4. Internal inconsistency: the conclusion mentions 'large models' as a highlighted topic, but no section discusses large models/LLMs. Bibliographic oddities: the XPINN reference author string is garbled in the online version ('Karniadakis A, Em G (2020)'; the actual XPINN paper is Jagtap & Karniadakis 2020, Commun Comput Phys 28(5):2002-2041, matching the cited volume/pages); received/accepted dates and corresponding author were not captured. Semantic Scholar counted 250 citations at analysis date vs the inventory's 358 (GS-snippet). FNO's absence from the operator-learning outlook is a genuine gap that our survey should note. This is the dossier's single most positioning-critical item: our differentiation rests on (i) industry/problem-class depth vs its three-paragraph application sketch, (ii) quantitative reliability evidence vs its narrative challenges section, and (iii) mechanism-level taxonomy vs its component lists.
